newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Weak Australian jobs data check 1997 optimism.
newsitem.headline: Weak Australian jobs data check 1997 optimism.

text.p: Australia on Thursday posted a slight rise in unemployment for February, in a timely reminder that the economy was not yet firing on all cylinders.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said employment fell by 7,200 in February, and the unemployment rate rose to 8.8 percent, equal to its highest level over the past two years.
The employment fall was in contrast to the median forecasts of a 10,000 rise in the month, and brought to an end a run of four successive rises in employment.
That in turn deflated some of the more optimistic hopes for the coming year and kept the prospect of an early rate hike off the agenda, economists said.
"The weak February employment report should help wind back some of the excessive optimism about the 1997 economic outlook," Nomura Research economists said in a report.
Economists said the fact that employment had fallen was not a concern as such, but did highlight that the labour market and activity was still quite slow at the beginning of the year.

Adding to that view was the ongoing weakness in full-time jobs, which fell 24,200 in February and are only up 5,900 on their level of 12 months ago. In contrast, part-time jobs rose by 17,000 over the month and are up 83,100 over the past year.

"Let's not get carried away with the growth story: 8.8 percent unemployment and the loss of 24,200 full time jobs in February suggests that economic growth will not be one-way traffic in 1997," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said.
Employment, seen as a lagging indicator of economic activity, is expected to slowly improve through 1997 but analysts saw only limited improvement in the unemployment rate.
"There will not be any sustainable pick up in employment, or a sustainable drop in the unemployment rate, until the second half of 1997," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said.
However, while the jobs data may have been a reality check for markets running away with the growth story, economists still expect a strengthening in the economy this year.

Supporting the prospects of improving activiy were housing finance data for Janaury, which were also realeased on Thursday. Housing finance approvals rose 5.0 percent in the month, matching their December rise and adding to the growing evidence of a recovery in the housing sector.
Approvals are now at their highest level since July 1994, and the continued strength in approvals for construction and the purchase of new dwellings was of most interest to economists.

"This recovery is not only important for the direct impact that housing construction makes to activity but also for the multiplier effect that it has through other sectors of the economy," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Tony Meer said.
These effects included increased demand for building materials and retail goods, as well for employment.
